title: Party Jollof Rice
author: Ozoz Adeniyi
desc: The deliberate-burn version: long grain parboiled twelve to fifteen minutes, foil under the lid twice, and three to five minutes on high at the end to make the smoke.
longDesc: This is party jollof written down as a technique rather than an accident. The rice is parboiled in stock until it is still hard, a bit white and only partly cooked, the pepper base is fried down until the raw tomato taste has gone, and the pot is covered with a double layer of foil or parchment under the lid — twice, once for each stage. Then comes the part that makes it party jollof: with the rice cooked, the heat goes up with the lid on and the rice is burnt for three to five minutes until it crackles and smells toasted. Rest thirty minutes minimum.
ingredients: 4 cups uncooked long-grain rice — not basmati
6 cups stock (vegetable, chicken or beef) or water, divided
6 medium fresh plum or Roma tomatoes, chopped, or a 400 g tin
6 fresh red poblano peppers, or 4 large red bell peppers, seeds discarded
3 medium red onions — 1 sliced thinly, 2 roughly chopped, divided
1 scotch bonnet pepper, yellow preferred, to taste
1/3 cup oil — vegetable, canola or coconut, not olive
2 tsp Caribbean or Jamaican-style curry powder
equipment: Heavy pot with a tight lid
steps: Rinse the rice, then parboil it with 2 cups of stock, covered, 12 to 15 minutes on medium heat. It should still be hard, a bit white rather than translucent, and only partly cooked.
Blend the tomatoes, poblano or bell peppers, chopped onions and scotch bonnet until smooth — about 4 cups in total.
Heat the oil, add the sliced onion with a pinch of salt and stir 1 to 2 minutes.
Add the tomato paste, curry powder, thyme and bay leaves and stir 2 minutes.
Add the blended mixture and cook 10 to 12 minutes on medium heat, until the raw tomato taste disappears.
Add 2 cups of stock and 1 teaspoon of butter, then the parboiled rice.
Stir, and cover with a double piece of foil, baking or parchment paper, then the lid. Cook on low 15 minutes.
Stir, adjust the seasoning, and add the remaining 1 cup of stock.
Re-cover with foil or parchment and the lid, and cook 15 to 20 minutes more, stirring every 10 minutes, until the grains separate. Add stock or water by the half-cup if needed.
For party jollof: with the rice cooked, turn the heat up with the lid on and burn it 3 to 5 minutes — the rice will crackle and smell toasted.
Turn off the heat, cover the top with a tea cloth, and rest a minimum of 30 minutes.
chefTips: Long grain, not basmati — the source rules it out explicitly. Note that the same author's other jollof prefers basmati, so this is a real disagreement between two recipes by one person.
Parboil to still hard and a bit white. If it looks cooked at this stage the finished jollof will be mush.
A double piece of foil or parchment under the lid, and twice — once for each cooking stage. It traps the steam far better than a lid alone.
The burn is deliberate. Heat up, lid on, three to five minutes, listening for the crackle. Longer under the lid means smokier rice.
Thirty minutes' rest, minimum, with a tea cloth over the top. The cloth absorbs the condensation that would otherwise drip back and wet the rice.
Caribbean or Jamaican-style curry powder is specified, and it is not the same product as Nigerian curry powder. Neither source treats them as substitutable.
Stock rather than water throughout, added in three stages — two cups, two cups, one cup, then half-cups as needed. That staging is what keeps the grains separate.
commonMistakes: Parboiling the rice until it is actually cooked.
Using a lid without the foil or parchment layer.
Adding all six cups of stock at once.
Burning it with the lid off, which dries it instead of smoking it.
sources: Adapted from 'Classic Nigerian Jollof Rice', published on Food52, 16 August 2016, credited to Kitchen Butterfly. ATTRIBUTION NOTE: pages on kitchenbutterfly.com byline as the site name rather than as Ozoz Sokoh, and the Food52 byline is the same site name; the site is credited, with Sokoh noted as proprietor. Yield as printed: a family-sized pot. Prep 30 minutes, cook 1 hour 30 minutes.

Quantities exactly as printed: 4 cups uncooked long-grain rice (not basmati); 6 cups stock (vegetable, chicken, or beef) or water, divided; 6 medium fresh plum/Roma tomatoes, chopped, OR 400-gram tin; 6 fresh red poblano peppers (or 4 large red bell peppers), seeds discarded; 3 medium red onions (1 sliced thinly, 2 roughly chopped), divided; 1 Scotch bonnet pepper (yellow preferred), to taste; 1/3 cup oil (vegetable/canola/coconut, not olive); 3 tablespoons tomato paste; 2 teaspoons Caribbean/Jamaican-style curry powder; 1 teaspoon (heaping) dried thyme; 2 dried bay leaves; 2 teaspoons unsalted butter (optional), divided; salt to taste.

Headnote as printed: 'Because Jollof Rice is Bae, and much loved South of the Sahara and along the coast of West Africa. Spiced and stewed in a flavorful tomato broth, it is everything from "everyday" to celebration.'
PARBOIL DONENESS CUE, verbatim: the rice should be 'still hard, a bit "white" (not translucent) and only partly cooked.'

THE DELIBERATE BURN, as printed: after the rice cooks, turn the heat up with the lid on and 'burn' 3 to 5 minutes — the rice crackles and smells toasted. Turn off the heat; rest with the lid on. LONGER LID COVERAGE EQUALS SMOKIER FLAVOUR. Rest minimum 30 minutes with a tea cloth over the top.

THE HEADLINE FINDING ACROSS THE THREE JOLLOFS, and it is not reconciled: the same author publishes a basmati, no-parboil, accidental-smoke jollof on her own site (NGA110) and this long-grain, parboiled, foil-lid, deliberate-burn jollof at Food52 — and this one EXPLICITLY RULES OUT the rice the other one prefers. These are two different dishes under one name, and this is the party-jollof technique document.

DISAGREEMENTS across all three documented versions. Rice type: 'long-grain, not basmati' here; 'long grain or basmati', personally basmati, on her own site; 'long grain parboiled' at All Nigerian Recipes (NGA111). Pre-treatment: rinse then parboil 12-15 minutes in stock here; rinse and pre-soak basmati 20+ minutes there; parboil THEN rinse and drain at ANR. Foil lid: double foil or parchment under the lid, twice, here; none there, lid only with a tea cloth at the end; not specified at ANR. Smoke: technique here, accident there, not described at ANR. Curry powder: 'Caribbean/Jamaican-style' here, unspecified type there, 'Nigerian curry powder' at ANR — and these are not the same products.

ON THE TOMATO-TO-PEPPER RATIO, three architectures and no agreement: 6 tomatoes to 6 red poblano to 1 scotch bonnet here, roughly even; 6 tomatoes to half a fresh chili and NO sweet pepper at all on her own site; entirely unquantified at ANR. A fourth, from a different author, gives it as percentages — roughly 50% bell pepper, 30% tomatoes, 15% onions, 5% scotch bonnet (NGA019).

HISTORICAL NOTE, recorded as a lead rather than a finding: the earliest documented jollof recipe is reported to be in 'Practical West African Cookery' (1910) by S. Leith-Ross and G. Ruxton, held by the Wellcome Library and freely available via the Internet Archive at archive.org/details/b28132762. 'Joloff rice' was confirmed to appear in a dinner-menu suggestion on page 34 — 'Pumpkin soup. Joloff rice. Lime sponge.' — and the recipe itself sits in the book's 'Macaroni and Rice' chapter, which lies past the point where the available text extract truncated. THE RECIPE TEXT WAS NOT RETRIEVED and nothing from it is reproduced here. Worth noting alongside it, from Ozoz Sokoh's own framing of that book's preface: its writers' 'main object in view was to enable the white man to obtain that well cooked and varied food so essential to health.' It is a manual for feeding colonial officers using African ingredients and African cooks — the earliest PRINTED jollof recipe, not the earliest one.
reheating: Steam, or microwave with a splash of water and a damp cover.
healthBenefits: Red bell pepper and tomato together give a high vitamin C and lycopene load.
Lower in fat than most party rice dishes at a third of a cup of oil for eight servings.
culturalNote: Party jollof is a genuinely different thing from household jollof, and the smoke is the difference — the burnt layer at the bottom of a huge pot cooked over firewood is what people queue for at a Nigerian party. That this recipe turns the accident into an instruction is its real contribution: heat up, lid on, three to five minutes, listen for the crackle.
